Title: Modeling desirable futures at local scale by combining the nature futures framework and multi-objective optimization
Intro: Operationalizing the Nature Futures Framework to Catalyze the Development of Nature-Future Scenarios
Description:
This study modelled desirable futures at local scale by combining the NFF and multi-objective optimisation. By doing so, they showcase how the NFF can guide quantitative scenario modelling and decision-making based on a protocol for operationalization of the NFF.

The protocol encompasses (1) exploring nature-positive futures, (2) seeking alternative pathways for targets satisfying visions of plural values, and (3) screening key direct drivers to achieve the targets.  This protocol is tested with a case study in the rural landscape of Bekambeushi River watershed in northeastern Japan.

LANDIS-II was used to model land use and land cover changes from 2015 to 2100 to explore desirable futures with plausible management strategies, focussing on nature-positive strategies. Then, Pareto optimal strategies are identified and transferred into NFF state space. By screening key management actions for forestry, farmland and renewables as pathways to match with the NFF categories, the work highlights trade-offs and synergies within different value perspectives.

The developed protocol can be used to explore how management strategies will contribute to desirable futures scenarios and its policy implications to reach a desirable state or transform a non-nature-positve strategy into a nature-positive strategy. Selective cutting was identified as the key response option for nature-positive futures.
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): 15 Life on Land
Scale: A large landscape or city scape (e.g. Sao Paulo <50 km on edge)
Resource 1 (Reference): Haga, C., Maeda, M., Hotta, W. et al. Modeling desirable futures at local scale by combining the nature futures framework and multi-objective optimization. Sustain Sci (2023)

Title: Developing multiscale and integrative nature–people scenarios using the Nature Futures Framework
Intro: The process for coming up with the Nature Futures Framework (NFF) as a flexible tool designed to support the development of scenarios and models of desirable futures for people, nature and Mother Earth.
Description:
There is a need for transformative, multiscale global scenarios as positive Nature Futures to protect biodiversity and achieve sustainability goals. In an interative and participatory process, lead by a group of experts from the IPBES, the Nature Futures Framework was develeoped to specifically create positive Nature Futures.

The workshop was structured in four steps. First, a photo exercise on participants' relationship to nature set the scene to create thematic groups. Second, three seeds per theme are selected and discovered with the method of Future Wheels. Afterwards, a three horizons diagramme per theme was created to visualize pathways towards the visions. Finally, the visions are mapped, focussing on topics and regions. This resulted in seven visions for positive Nature Futures on the topics of state of biodiversity, value of nature, management of nature, governance systems, production and consumption of ecosystem services, socio-economic development, use of technology and lifestyles. All of the visions require a societal paradigm shift and significant changes in values towards ‘responsible stewardship’ relationship between people and nature. these visions were further tested and refined through stakeholder engagement in different context.
Impact:
Based on the seven visions, a group of experts identified three underlying value perspectives which were then brought together in the Natures Futures Framework (NFF) triangle. The "Nature for Nature" dimension encompasses intrinsic values of nature. Instrumental values such as Nature's Contribution for People and Ecosystem Services are reflected in "Nature for Society". The perspective "Nature as Culture" represents relational values in living in harmony with nature.

Through further stakeholder engagement processes and testing it was concluded that a plural values perspective is rather oriented towards the center space of the triangle while thriving for balance and harmony in some sectors might require a stronger orientation towards the corners of the triangle. The NFF triangle serves as a boundary object for plural values in desirable Nture futures on multiple scales to inform decision-making

From this process, a task force on scenarios and models to advance work on scenarios and models of biodiversity and ecosystem functions and services, as part of the new IPBES work programme up to 2030 is developing six illustrative scenarios of futures based on an extreme interpretation of the three value perspectives and the edges where they intersect.
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): 13 Climate Action|16 Peace Justice and Strong Institutions|17 Partnerships to achieve the Goals
Scale: Global
Theme(s): Climate change|Nature’s contributions to people|NFF|Transformative change
Resource 1 (Reference): Research article on workshops and development of the NFF
Resource 2 (Reference): Research article on modelling Nature Futures

Title: The voices of youth in envisioning positive futures for nature and people
Intro: We offer these visions as a starting point for opening up the conversation about what desirable futures might look like from the perspective of young people.
Description:
During the first IPBES youth workshop in 2019, held in São Pedro, Brazil, 33 early-career individuals cam together to explore positive futures of biodiversity and ecosystem services. On the one hand, this process addressed the need to include the perspective of the youth from 23 different countries into futures thinking and decision-making. On the other hand, this is only the starting point of valuable contribution by youth from around the world to IPBES's work and scenario planing. The NFF triangle was used as an activation tool to familiarize with the framework, think in diverse value perspectives and create four interest-driven groups for the following visioning exercises. Cities, rural landscapes and coastal ecosystems were assigned as broader topics to each group. Afterwards, the groups worked with seeds to envision the future. Methods such as naming the vision, creating a tweet and newspaper headline as well as in-depth questioned added detail to the visions while they were graphically depiced by ocal artists. The groups came up with four visions:
  1. Anthropocene 2.0, representing the centre of the NFF triangle and focussing on coastal landscapes
  2. Econetlands = representing the Nature as Culture perspective and centre of the NFF triangle with the focus on cities
  3. Rural Transformers = representing the Nature for Society perspective and focussing on rural landscapes
  4. Iandé Etama = representing the Nature for Nature perspective with the focus on rural landscapes
Impact:
All visions aim for a value shift towards sustainable and equitable societies in which alternatives to the current capitalis paradigm, such as circularity and sharing economy, are persued. Generally, mellenials are open to technology which is as well reflected in their visions with various technological aspects in contrast to the scenario archetypes by the IPBES.

A key finding of this process was that engaging early career professionals in participatory visioning exercises is of extreme relevance in the political-scientific context of coproduction of science and solutions.

Ecosystem(s): Coastal/marine areas|Small scale agriculture & villages|Urban and suburban
Scale: Global

Title: Exploring citizen scientists' values through the Nature Futures Framework
Intro: This case describes how the NFF was used to make visible the diverse values in relation to nature that are expressed and fostered through the New Zealand Garden Bird Survey.
Description:
The New Zealand Garden Bird Survey (NZGBS) is an annual citizen science event where participants count the maximum number and type of birds they see or hear in their communities. The bird counts are then used to calculate how bird populations change over 5- and 10-year timeframes at different spatial scales across New Zealand.

Most citizen science evaluation focuses on making sure citizens do the science right and stay doing it. While this is important, we were interested in understanding the outcomes fostered through the NZGBS, and how this prompts impacts at individual and collective scales. We used the NFF to make visible the diverse human-nature values that prompt participation in, and are expressed through, counting and reporting birds.

Some NZGBS participants highlighted the intrinsic value and beauty of birds (nature for nature). They described how participation in the NZGBS reminds them of this intrinsic value, and the resourcing that goes into the dataset reflects this intrinsic value. Other participants highlighted the human wellbeing outcomes of doing the NZGBS (nature for society). These benefits included the emotional or affective experiences such as joy, amusement, feeling calm or relaxed, and being entertained and curious. Finally, other participants described how observing and counting birds makes them feel connected to both nature and other people who care about these matters in New Zealand (nature as culture). Many of these participants emphasised how the NZGBS both reminded, and enabled them, to express care for nature in a collective effort that involved other people who share this value.

In this example the NFF lens helped create greater visibility for the relational (nature as culture) aspects citizen science can foster - both between people and nature - and between people. Most citizen science projects and associated evaluations are good at theorising the values in the NFF related to nature for nature (science about nature) and to nature for society (ecosystem services and wellbeing benefits). They are less well equipped to evaluate nature as culture. The NFF can help nature-based citizen science projects to better accommodate all perspectives to contribute to building the people-nature connection that is urgently needed to address pressing social and environmental challenges.
Impact: The study has been used to better understand the link between citizen science and action to support nature. Our analysis shows that citizen science projects like the NZGBS do not require people to agree on, or to even articulate, a shared set of values before they can participate. Rather, through the collective practice of doing something (like observing and counting birds), citizen science projects can contribute to a wider network of people and groups who actively shape the valuing of biodiversity in specific contexts.

Scale: Medium country (e.g. Zimbabwe or Germany 201-2000 km)

Title: The Urban Nature Futures Framework (UNFF)
Intro: We adapted the NFF for the urban century by integrating multiple values into urban management
Description:
It is widely known that the planetary health is interlinked with the balance between rapidly growing cities and its impacts on the natural environment. Since it is projected that future urban expansion will have pressurs on ecological integrity, there is the needto combine future urban growth with biodiversity conservation in working towards the vision “humanity living in harmony with nature”. Therefore the Nature Futures Framework was adapted to integrate nature values into participatory urban planning. The proposed UNFF acknowledges nature as integral part of urban planning that shapes the structure of a city while accounting for equity and environmental justice. The aim is to create multiple positive visions for nature in cities, enabling decision-makers, planners, institutions, and urban dwellers to explore multiple transformative pathways for sustainable cities. Based on that, three contrasting visions for each value corner of the NFF are developed.
  1. Nature for Nature future: giving space for natural areas and biodiversity within cities while keeping human impact minimal
  2. Nature for Society: enhancing Nature's Contributions to People/ ecosystem services with green and blue infrastructure
  3. Nature as Culture: securing equitable access to nature for recreation and space for cultural enjoyment in multiple ways
These visions support the implementation of the UNFF along four key components.
  1. Identifying and leveraging socio-ecological feedbacks
  2. Assessing indirect impacts
  3. Establishing monitoring frameworks
  4. Developing scenarios
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): 11 Sustainable Cities and Communities|13 Climate Action|15 Life on Land
Scale: Global

Title: Nature recovery on the Downland Estate, Brighton and Hove
Intro: This study uses the Nature Futures Framework to assess nature recovery strategies on Brighton and Hove's Downland Estate.
Description:
The aim of the project was to better understand how stakeholders relate to different land management scenarios. We assessed the perceived performance of alternative nature recovery options across Nature Future (NF) value perspectives and between contrasting stakeholder groups.

The scenarios were developed based on existing literature and expert assessment, and aimed to cover the range of NF perspectives.

The results of this study showed a diverse range of preferences for land use on the Downland Estate. Generally, participants seemed open to change and nature recovery. There was no clear best performing scenario across all NF perspectives.
Impact: At the time of the study a new management plan for the Downland Estate was under consideration by Brighton and Hove council.

Title: An Ocean of Possibilities: Imagining the Future of Ocean Sustainability
Intro: Five visioning scenarios exploring the future of ocean sustainability from the perspective of a diversity of actors.
Description:
The Ocean of Possibilities project was conducted between 2023 and 2025 by the Ocean & Climate Platform (OCP), together with the National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) and Friends of Ocean Action (FOA), and with the support of Dona Bertarelli Philanthropy. Developed as part of the OCP’s mandate to mobilise, consult and amplify the voices of civil society in preparation for the third UN Ocean Conference (UNOC 3), the project aimed to develop a collective vision from civil society of a sustainable and regenerative ocean future. Grounded in a “visioning” methodology—a scientific approach designed to collectively imagine desirable futures and identify concrete pathways to realise them—the project engaged diverse civil society members through global consultations, workshops, and interviews. The project led to the development of five distinct visions of a desirable future for the ocean, with concrete actions to achieve them. Three key messages emerge from these scenarios:
  • An ocean of possibilities: There is no single desirable future for the ocean, but many possible ones. Despite these differences, there are common actions, such as strengthening ocean protection, decarbonisation, and ocean literacy, that must be prioritised to unlock transformative change.
  • A role for all: Change can happen through both incremental and radical actions, which should be led by clearly defined actors. Responsibility is shared across actors and scales, and every contribution matters in shaping a just and regenerative ocean future.
  • A united ocean community: The ocean community is united around shared principles: justice, knowledge, accountability, care for the ocean, and solidarity. Ocean action is a catalyst for positive change across sectors as it enables broader societal benefits like equity, peace, and sustainable development.
Impact: The results were shared at the third UN Ocean Conference (UNOC 3) in Nice. A collective call for action was published: https://sdg.iisd.org/commentary/guest-articles/our-blue-future-a-call-for-action-from-the-ocean-community/

Title: Using the Nature Futures Framework as a lens for developing plural land use scenarios for Europe for 2050
Intro:
Ambitious international biodiversity targets, like the EU’s Green Deal, lack clear land-use pathways. To address this, we introduce a novel approach using the Nature Futures Framework (NFF) to assess how sustainability targets might be spatially implemented based on the diverse ways society values nature. Using the CLUMondo model, we simulated land system scenarios for Europe in 2050, accounting for projected population trends and commodity demands.

We created three scenarios that successfully meet sustainability targets, each reflecting a specific NFF value: Nature for Society (focus on climate regulation), Nature for Nature(focus on species conservation), or Nature as Culture (focus on agricultural heritage).
Description:
The scenario project aims to explore the spatial and land-system consequences of achieving ambitious international biodiversity targets - such as the EU Green Deal and CBD - across Europe by 2050.

A primary goal is to address the uncertainty of how these broad sustainability targets can be physically implemented on the ground. To do so, the IPBES Nature Futures Framework (NFF) were translated into spatially explicit simulations using the CLUMondo model. Instead of forecasting a single trajectory, the project seeks to model "plural" pathways that reflect different normative ways society values nature: for its intrinsic value (Nature for Nature), its practical utility (Nature for Society), or its cultural heritage (Nature as Culture).

Results indicate that achieving these targets requires drastic land system changes across all perspectives. Natural forests and grasslands are forecast to expand, while productive areas will undergo simultaneous intensification and diversification. Although the overall direction of change is similar, 20% of Europe's land area will differ depending on the adopted NFF perspective, with prominent spatial disagreements emerging in eastern and western Europe.
Impact: By modeling these alternative futures, the project aims to quantify the complex trade-offs and synergies in land management, such as balancing the expansion of natural habitats with the need for agricultural production. Ultimately, the goal is to map areas of spatial convergence—where all value systems require similar land changes—and hotspots of contention. Highlighting these spatial realities is intended to foster constructive dialogue among policymakers and stakeholders, providing an evidence-based tool for managing land sustainably.

Title: Ten scenarios on reindeer herding and land use in northern Finland
Intro: Reindeer herding is a traditional nature-based livelihood practiced in Finland by indigenous Saami people and ethnic Finn herders. It is impacted by range of cumulative pressures (e.g. land use, climate change, nature conservation / restoration, geopolitics.. etc).
Description: The aim of our scenario study was to diversify SSPs / exploratory scenario archetypes by introducing a systematic scenario assessment approach relating to assumptions on plausible future governance modes. The idea is that SSPs / scenario archetypes and chosen governance modes form a scenario matrix providing a logic for scenario narratives in each cell of the matrix. This approach was employed regarding reindeer herding in Finland, and led to development of 10 scenario storylines for reindeer futures. The work started with perspective paper Sarkki et al. 2023 who developed 3 scenario skeletons within Sustainability scenario archetype / SSP 1. The work was complemented in a research paper Sarkki et al. 2025, focusing to the reindeer case in more detail. Annex of that paper (Sarkki et al. 2025) includes the 10 reindeer futures storylines. Conceptually, the scenario approach to diversify SSPs was published in Sarkki et al. 2026.
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): 10 Reduced Inequality|16 Peace Justice and Strong Institutions
Scale: Small country (e.g. Trinidad or Cape Verde 50-200 km on edge)

Title: A Preliminary Study on Scenarios for Biodiversity Targets in China Based on the "Nature Futures Framework"
Subnational Region: Rather than focusing on specific administrative divisions such as provinces, prefectures, or districts, this study covers regions at varying stages of development—including urban, peri‑urban, and coastal zones—thereby supporting multi‑scale analysis across diverse socioeconomic and ecological contexts in China
Case Contributor: YU Dan-dan,  TONG Wen-jun,  LIU Wei,  YI Jian-feng,  CHEN Meng-meng,  CAO Ming-chang,  XU Hai-gen
Intro: Here, we review the methodological process of developing scenario narratives, propose the key points for creating scenarios of biodiversity targets in China and establish three sets of positive scenarios for “Beautiful China”, “Harmonious China” and “Smart China” based on the “NFF framework”
Description:
Addressing the limitations of conventional biodiversity scenarios—which predominantly focus on projecting future trends of anthropogenic drivers (e.g., climate change, land-use change) and their adverse impacts on nature, while inadequately capturing the plural values of nature-human relationships, cross-scale linkages, and synergies and trade-offs between biodiversity conservation targets and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development—this study applies the IPBES Nature Futures Framework (NFF) to fill the critical gap in NFF-based subglobal case studies. Specific objectives are to:
  • systematize the methodological workflow for developing NFF-aligned scenario narratives tailored to the national context, through a review of international best practices and iterative, multi-stakeholder consultations involving researchers, policymakers and local practitioners
  • co-develop three positive, policy-relevant biodiversity conservation scenarios for China (“Beautiful China”, “Harmonious China” and “Smart China”) aligned with the NFF’s three core value perspectives (intrinsic, instrumental and relational values of nature), with target years set to 2035 and 2050 to synchronize with China’s medium- and long-term national development planning horizons
  • and provide robust scientific and technical support for the formulation, implementation and evaluation of national biodiversity conservation targets, facilitate China’s effective implementation of the post-2020 Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF), and contribute empirical evidence to refine the NFF for broader multi-scale application.
Impact:
This study represents a pivotal methodological and empirical contribution to the application of the IPBES Nature Futures Framework (NFF) at the national scale, with implications spanning academic, policy, and science‑policy interface dimensions.
  • Filling a Critical Gap in National‑Scale NFF Applications. Prior to this study, NFF‑based scenario exercises remained overwhelmingly concentrated at the global scale, while national and sub‑national case studies—essential for ensuring the diversity and inclusiveness of future scenarios—were scarce, particularly for China. By systematically adapting the NFF's iterative, participatory scenario‑design methodology to the Chinese context, the study established the first NFF‑aligned national biodiversity conservation target scenarios for China, directly responding to the IPBES call for urgent multi‑level case studies at regional and national scales.
  • Operationalizing the Three Value Perspectives of Nature. The study translated the NFF's three core value perspectives—intrinsic (nature for nature), relational (nature as culture), and instrumental (nature for society)—into three concrete, policy‑relevant positive scenarios: "Beautiful China," "Harmonious China," and "Smart China". This tripartite scenario architecture provides a navigation tool for Chinese policymakers to conceptualize and compare alternative biodiversity futures, enabling a more transparent discussion of synergies and trade‑offs between conservation targets and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
  • Supporting the Implementation of the Post‑2020 Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF)By aligning . scenario time horizons (2035 and 2050) with China's medium‑ and long‑term national development planning cycles, the study provides a science‑based foundation for translating the Kunming‑Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework into national targets. The NFF‑based scenario approach directly supports the GBF's ambition to "live in harmony with nature" and offers a methodological template for other Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity undertaking similar national target‑setting exercises.
  • Catalyzing Subsequent Quantitative Modeling and Multi‑Scale Extensions. While the study itself delivers qualitative scenario narratives, it has served as a methodological catalyst for downstream quantitative research. Subsequent work—exemplified by the Zhejiang provincial land‑use and biodiversity modeling study (2024)—explicitly adopted the "Beautiful China" and "Smart China" scenario logics to quantitatively simulate land‑use patterns and Mean Species Abundance (MSA) under the FLUS‑Biodiversity model. This demonstrates the study's ripple effect in bridging qualitative NFF narratives with quantitative scenario modeling, addressing one of the key research frontiers identified within the paper itself.
  • Advancing the Science‑Policy Interface for Ecological Civilization. The study contributes to the conceptual operationalization of China's "Ecological Civilization" paradigm by demonstrating how plural values of nature can be systematically integrated into national biodiversity governance. Through multi‑stakeholder consultation involving researchers, policymakers, and local practitioners, it exemplifies the co‑production of knowledge that IPBES promotes, thereby strengthening the science‑policy interface for biodiversity decision‑making in China.
  • Informing Iterative Refinement of the NFF Itself. As an early national‑scale empirical application, the study generates context‑specific feedback for the ongoing refinement of the NFF and its methodological guidance . The challenges it identifies—such as the need for systematic scenario‑development guidelines, integration of qualitative narratives with quantitative models, and enhanced multi‑scale policy alignment—directly inform the IPBES task force on scenarios and models as it continues to evolve the framework for broader global application.
In essence, the study's principal impact lies in its role as a bridge‑builder: between the global NFF methodology and national‑scale biodiversity governance; between qualitative visioning and quantitative modeling; and between China's Ecological Civilization discourse and the international GBF implementation agenda. While the scenarios themselves remain aspirational narratives pending full quantitative validation, they have already demonstrated concrete influence by shaping subsequent provincial‑scale modeling efforts and providing a replicable methodological template for NFF‑based national target‑setting worldwide.

Title: Challenges on the horizon: future scenarios and plant invasions in Aotearoa New Zealand
Intro: We explore how aspirational biocultural diversity policies and climate change could affect economic, social and environmental dynamics and the range of potential consequences for conservation.
Description:
Large scale changes in biodiversity and conservation management require long-term goals and planning across multiple sectors in the face of increasing global change, but responses are still often short-term and fragmented across agencies and sectors. Scenario-building can be a powerful tool to imagine possible futures, integrating across sectors and disciplines and promoting long-term thinking and planning. As an interdisciplinary team of experts, we developed potential scenarios for a range of future environmental conditions. The scenarios explored: increasing land ownership and stewardship of land by indigenous peoples (Māori); widespread reforestation using native tree species; national-scale eradication of invasive mammalian predators; and increasing frequency of extreme weather events. We explored the environmental, economic, social and policy implications of these globally-relevant trends at a national scale using Aotearoa New Zealand as our study system. Each scenario presented both opportunities and risks to equality, indigenous empowerment and human capital, emphasizing the importance of good policy responses to maximize benefits and minimize unintended harm. Across scenarios several common themes were consistently highlighted, including the importance of land use in driving other conservation outcomes. How the value of ecosystem services is recognized and prioritized was also important to a wide range of outcomes.

These four non-exclusive scenarios were then used to forecast trajectories of plant invasions into natural areas by 2050 and identify research gaps and future management needs. Under each scenario we considered socio-economic and ecological drivers such as changes in land use and biotic interactions, focussing on public and private conservation areas. For a scenario considering increased land ownership or stewardship by Indigenous people, sociological research around bicultural communication was key to meet expected management needs. Under increased native reforestation, research into the impacts of landscape connectivity and long-term resilience of restoration plantings was highlighted. With non-native mammalian predator eradication, identifying the impact of species’ removal from ecological networks and plant traits that promote success will be essential to identify emerging invaders. Increases in extreme weather events will disrupt management and spread ruderal invaders, requiring the development of better decision-making and prioritization tools. Several priorities emerged across all scenarios, including the need for research and data advances, better management tools, and improved communication and consensus-building. Investment in these areas provides long-term benefits across a range of possible futures.
Impact: The four scenarios we developed have been shared with stakeholders, including policy makers and practitioners, through a combination of online workshops, conferences and publications, as well as press releases. Stakeholders have expressed interest in and support for the themes and issues raised by the scenarios, and the needs we identified through the scenario-building and analysing process. The scenarios and gaps highlighted by the work can be used to support the development of future research programmes, while the methods used to generate and analyse the scenarios have been shared so that similar exercises can be conducted elsewhere.

Title: Transformation towards good governance in small-scale fisheries territory under ocean grabbing
Subnational Region: Baixada Santista Metropolitan Region, São Paulo State
Case Contributor: Ingrid Cabral Machado and Mayra Jankowsky
Intro: Participatory scenario planning facilitated fishers' and stakeholders' co-design of governance strategies for a viable future of small-scale fisheries territory affected by ocean grabbing driven by Latin America's largest port.
Description:
The participatory scenario planning was part of a research process conducted in a small-scale fishery territory overlapping with the Port of Santos, where port facilities, disasters and dredging generate pressures that challenge the viability of SSF. The broader research aimed to understand the implications of overlapping territories, characterize ocean grabbing dynamics and governance arrangements, and co-develop strategies for a viable future of the fishery.
The research involved three interconnected phases: (1) focus-group workshops with fishers to identify and characterize the multiple dimensions of ocean grabbing; (2) semi-structured interviews with key institutional stakeholders to complement this characterization and analyze territorial governance; and (3) a participatory scenario workshop bringing together fishers and stakeholders to explore possible futures for SSF.
Based on the previous phases, two future scenarios were developed and illustrated through art: a “viability” scenario, in which SSF remains possible as a livelihood, and a “collapse” scenario, reflecting current trends that could compromise its continuity. Participants selected the “viability” scenario and co-developed strategies and an action plan focused on key governance domains: negotiation mechanisms, environmental licensing, social participation, and regulation of port activities. The entire process was analyzed through the Interactive Governance framework.
The results showed that participatory scenario planning enabled the integration of different forms of knowledge and identified governance changes needed to shift from a trajectory of decline towards a viable future for SSF. The process highlighted that ensuring the continuity of SSF depends on governance mechanisms capable of addressing competing territorial uses. The study demonstrates the potential of participatory scenarios as a tool to support governance transitions in contexts of ocean grabbing.
Impact: The impacts of this work are still emerging, as the transition towards the selected viability scenario depends on strengthening fishers’ collective organization and fostering greater commitment from decision-making institutions. Despite this, the process represented a significant step by bringing together fishers and key institutional actors in an unprecedented participatory process addressing the socio-environmental conflict between small-scale fisheries and port activities, with a focus on pathways for SSF viability. The workshop contributed to making conflicts, priorities, and governance gaps more explicit, while providing a basis for future dialogue and negotiation. Thus, participatory scenario planning proved valuable not only for envisioning alternative futures, but also for identifying the institutional and social conditions required to move towards a more viable and equitable governance pathway.

Title: Participatory scenarios and spatial modelling to explore mangrove  ecosystem services futures in Lamu, Kenya
Intro: Participatory scenarios assessing how land use change affects mangrove ecosystem service value in Lamu, Kenya. Findings show governance quality, not mangrove area alone, shapes future outcomes to 2063.
Description:
This study used the Kesho participatory approach to co-produce four alternative land use scenarios for Lamu County, Kenya, looking ahead to 2063. A three-day workshop brought together 32 stakeholders, including government, NGOs, researchers, and community members such as fishers, mangrove harvesters, farmers, and tourism operators. Together they identified coastal development and environmental health as the two most important and uncertain drivers of change. These became the axes of a 2x2 scenario matrix, producing four narratives: New Dawn, Struggling Futures, Ecosystem Under Siege, and Growth Trap.

The scenarios were then translated into spatially explicit land cover maps using satellite data and modelling in TerrSet. A benefit transfer method was used to estimate how mangrove ecosystem services, including provisioning, regulating, and cultural services, might change under each scenario. The results show that governance quality and ecosystem condition matter more than mangrove area alone in determining the future value of these services.
Impact: This study presents the first participatory scenario assessment in Lamu County, providing policy-relevant insights into how development pathways may shape mangrove ecosystems and the services they provide. Beyond Lamu, Kesho offers an adaptable tool for application in other mangrove-rich regions globally, supporting efforts to align local decision-making with continental and global sustainability agendas.

Title: Mare Autonomia - Post-growth Ocean futures
Intro: A coherent post-growth future scenario for Ocean Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction (Mare Autonomia) meant to challenge the dominant Mare Liberum (freedom of the seas) imaginary of open ocean governance.
Description: Despite growing awareness that the pursuit of endless economic growth is the main driver of expansion and intensification of destructive practices, future scenarios for the Ocean often lack explicit critique of transnational capitalism. We expand the field by developing a post-growth future scenario for Ocean Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction (ABNJ). We employed Science-Fiction (SciFi) prototyping to explore how “seeds” of post-growth thinking in current legislation could disrupt traditional open Ocean governance. The scenario consists of four SciFi short stories (windows into the future, or scenario “vignettes”) concerning shipping, fishing, marine biotechnology and deep-sea mining, and a prototype Ocean treaty describing underlying governance principles.
Impact: Subjecting the scenario to experts allowed us to uncover imaginaries linked to the dominant growth paradigm hindering interviewees from seeing our scenario as a plausible Ocean future and illustrated the importance of relational imagination in envisioning radically different futures. We conclude that a business-as-usual Ocean future is not inherently more plausible than a post-growth Ocean future, and that engaging with creative scenarios can improve our capabilities in critically reflecting over the stories told about our present to de-naturalise the injustices they allow for.

Title: Future Workshop on German Coastal Fisheries 2045
Subnational Region: German Baltic Sea and North Sea Coast
Intro: Coastal fisheries in Germany are undergoing significant structural changes. Key challenges include the declining productivity of commercially important fish and shellfish stocks, the loss of traditional fishing grounds, a dwindling interest of the younger generation to become fishers, high fuel prices, and an aging fishing fleet. In this context, a workshop was convened to develop a future vision for German coastal fisheries.
Description: The Future Workshop on Coastal Fisheries 2045 aimed to develop a shared and desirable vision for the future of German coastal fisheries together with a diverse group of stakeholders: the workshop brought together different perspectives and forms of practical knowledge, involving actors from commercial and recreational fisheries, nature conservation, tourism, science, politics, fish wholesaling, and marine spatial planning. The Future Workshop aimed at turning stakeholders from actors primarily affected by the ongoing transformation into active participants in shaping future change. Rather than predicting what fisheries would most likely look like in 2045, the workshop followed a normative approach, asking participants to imagine how coastal fisheries should develop in the future. The Future Workshop was designed to foster dialogue across conflicting interest and collaboration in order to create a shared vision, supported by creative methods such as graphic recording. At first the group jointly reflected on the current challenges facing fisheries in the North and Baltic Seas. Building on this critique, participants were encouraged to move beyond existing constraints and develop a positive future scenario. Finally, the workshop identified key elements of a future coastal fisheries system, providing a basis for discussing possible pathways towards a sustainable, economically viable, and multi-use marine future.
Impact: The scenarios were part of a scientific project but happened before, resp. at the same time as political processes on the future of fisheries in Germany. The developed scenario was presented to the respective political committees and could therefore inform the policy advice on the future of German fisheries. It also continues to be consulted by the meanwhile established German Information and Coordination Centre for Fisheries Transformation.

Title: Role of agency in envisioning future human-nature relationships in the context of road infrastructure development in the Kavango-Zambezi region, Namibia
Intro: Using the Nature Futures Framework (NFF), we worked with local communities in Namibia to create probable and desirable future scenarios in the context of the ongoing road infrastructure development in the Kavango-Zambezi corridor.
Description: Using participatory mapping as a tool of collective visualization of the futures that the community desired versus those that are probable, amidst road development, we aimed to understand the role of agency (their influence) in defining the land use and development patterns of their surroundings. Simply, if the desired visuals differ significantly from the probable one, we argue then that the locals thought they had little influence in how their surroundings and land use will unfold, in future. Furthermore, based on their proximity to roads, we examined how communities valued nature: Nature for Nature, Nature for Society and Nature for Culture.
Impact: The study brought together diverse groups (based on age, gender, education levels, local leaders and samll-scale farmers) to debate, imagine and visualize their 'futures'. The exercise was also a reminder of their relationship with nature - stuff that they took for granted such as Nature's provisioning and its role in their culture.

Title: Conflict Futures: exploring the future of fishery conflict through narrative scenarios
Intro: Fisheries conflicts are projected to increase due to changes in our ocean. We consider how multiple causal factors can drive conflict using a scenario approach. We construct four scenarios in conflict-prone regions of the world. Questions sparked by the scenarios can help build anticipatory governance capacity.
Description:
Disruptive changes in our global ocean and fisheries have sparked warnings of an increase in fisheries conflicts. However, such environmental changes have not yet been considered in tandem with other critical social, economic and political trends to map out possible future trajectories for fisheries conflict. By systematically combining scientific evidence with creative story-telling techniques, we map out the different causal drivers of fisheries conflicts, and explore how they interact in four regional settings by developing four narrative scenarios. We advance the narrative scenario approach by combining diverse data sources to craft primary storylines, and by consulting regional experts to validate the scenarios and develop alternative future trajectories. By use of an exploratory scenario approach, we escape deterministic forecasts of future conflict and instead provide creative and complex narratives set in four regions of the world. The scenarios are:
  • the North-East Atlantic: "Scramble for the Atlantic" (2030)
  • the East China Sea: "Remodeled Empire" (2045)
  • the coast of West Africa: "Oceanic Decolonization" (2045)
  • the Arctic Ocean: "Polar Renaissance" (2060)
We highlight key lessons learnt from the four scenarios, and the narrative approach taken to build them, for both scientists and policymakers. The scenarios are designed to trigger questions around the consequences of our current choices and how to avoid undesirable trajectories. They can be used to support decision making in the present by building capacity for better anticipation of an unpredictable future

Title: Scenarios for Baltic herring fisheries
Intro: Normative and exploratory scenarios for the use of Baltic herring
Description:
The project built exploratory and normative scenarios for Baltic herring fisheries with specific focus on the integration food security and safety aspects into the management of Baltic herring fisheries. Exploratory scenarios were built for the future of Baltic herring fisheries using 2040 as the target year. Four contrasting storylines were created based on two key uncertainties related to governance integration and environmental awareness. Policy documents, other scenario studies, and literature on the dynamics of Baltic fisheries were used as primary material. Backcasting, which is a normative scenario method, was used to define desirable future visions for the use of Baltic herring catch and to develop pathways of actor-specific governance actions to increase the use of the fish as a safe-to-eat food. The participatory backcasting exercise was organised as part of a two-day expert workshop in 2016. Workshop participants included eleven fisheries and dioxin experts across sectors and Baltic Sea riparian countries.

The scenario work produced three main publications: 1) Pihlajamäki et al. (2018) presents the results of the participatory backcasting exercise, i.e. pathways to increase the use of Baltic herring as safee-to-eat fish; 2) Sarkki and Pihlajamäki (2019) explores how backcasting recommendations work across the exploratory storyline; and 3) Pihlajamäki et al. (2020) apply Bayesian belief networks to exploratory scenario storylines to assess long-term changes in Baltic herring and salmon fisheries.

The scenarios were part of BONUS+ GOHERR (Integrated governance of Baltic herring and salmon stocks involving stakeholders) project (2015-2018).

Title: Positive futures for Litoral Norte marine protected area in Portugal
Intro: A participatory workshop where fishers, tourism operators, managers and scientists co-created visions for 2030 of Litoral Norte, a marine protected area in northern Portugal.

In fact, there is now a strategic council where resource users actively participate in the MPA’s conservation decisions. It also opened a rare space for dialogue among institutions and scientists who rarely discussed the MPA together, and gave participants a clearer understanding of one another's difficulties, needs and visions for its future.

Title: Co-creating positive narratives for small-scale fisheries in Europe
Intro: This case study is a one-day (5h) visioning exercise implemented during a longer workshop (1 week / IYAFA Regional Workshop: Getting the Story Straight and Envisioning a Fair Future for Small-Scale Fisheries in Europe) with small-scale fishers from across Europe, organized by the LIFE Platform, ICSF, and Mulleres Salgadas.
Description: The main goal of this visioning exercise was to develop desirable narratives and visions for small-scale fisheries in Europe by engaging workshop participants in a creative, interactive, and inspiring co-creation process. In addition, the exercise aimed to help participants feel more hopeful, counteracting the sense of being overwhelmed by the crises facing small-scale fisheries, and to set the scene for the workshop sessions that followed (which were not directly related to futures co-creation). To do this, we combined several approaches and futures-related methods (Seeds of Good Anthropocenes, the Manoa Mash-Up method), along with the use of personas, in a participatory setting involving small-scale fishers and their representatives. During the workshop, an artist captured emerging ideas to develop an illustration summarizing the session, which was later shared with all participants.

Title: Envisioning nature-positive futures for Europe using a nexus approach
Intro:
This study co-created plural nature-positive futures for Europe in 2050
that leverage synergies within the biodiversity nexus. The process
involved a 2-day co-creation workshop with 26 participants from across Europe, and a 2-hour virtual workshop.
Description:
The main goal was to co-create nature futures for Europe with 26
participants representing diverse sectors and regions, resulting in three
visions underpinned by different value perspectives: Dòigh Nàdair: The
way of nature (Nature as Culture), NaturAll (Nature for Nature) and Return
to Nature (Nature for Society). The rationale for this work was that
transformative change is required to secure a liveable future for people
and nature. The Nature Futures Framework and nexus approaches
together offer useful ways of imagining plural values of nature and the
foundational role of biodiversity across the biodiversity nexus together.
So, we brought these areas of biodiversity research together to ask: what
could plural nature-positive futures for Europe in 2050 look like that
explicitly leverage synergies in the biodiversity nexus?
Impact: These visions were used to inspire transformative pathways that were co-created in two subsequent workshops with a consistent group of participants in Schoorl, Netherlands and Teplice, Greece. These pathways identify sequences of actions that together may move to the desirable endpoints described in the visions.

Title: Indigenous and local knowledge in exploring the desirable futures of the mangrove ecosystem sustainability in the Mono Transboundary Biosphere Reserve, West Africa.
Intro: The project brought together Indigenous and local perspectives to envision desirable futures for mangrove ecosystems and identify transformation pathways towards sustainability in the Mono Transboundary Biosphere Reserve, West Africa.
Description: This project investigates how Indigenous and Local Knowledge (ILK) can contribute to desirable futures for mangrove ecosystem sustainability in the Mono Transboundary Biosphere Reserve (MTBR), West Africa. It documents ILK practices, their associated benefits and threats, and explores their transformative potential for co-developing qualitative and imaginative visions and locally grounded transformation pathways towards desirable and sustainable mangrove futures in the MTBR.
Impact:
The key impacts of this research can be framed around knowledge, practice, governance, conservation, and transformative change.
  • Recognition and valorization of Indigenous and Local Knowledge (ILK): Strengthens recognition of local knowledge, practices, values, and institutions as important resources for mangrove conservation and sustainability.
  • Locally grounded visions of desirable futures: Provides qualitative and imaginative desirable future visions that reflect the aspirations, values, and worldviews of communities and other stakeholders in the MTBR.
  • Transformation pathways for mangrove sustainability: Identifies practical transformation pathways for moving from current challenges towards desirable futures.
  • More inclusive conservation governance: Highlights the importance of involving Indigenous peoples and local communities, women, youth, Indigenous authorities, and other stakeholders in shaping mangrove futures and decision-making.
  • Bridging knowledge systems: Demonstrates how ILK can complement scientific knowledge and contribute to more context-sensitive approaches to biodiversity conservation and ecosystem management.
  • Policy and management relevance: Generates evidence that can inform mangrove conservation policies, participatory management strategies, restoration initiatives, and biodiversity governance within the MTBR and potentially other West African coastal landscapes.
  • Methodological innovation: Demonstrates the value of combining participatory visioning approaches such as the Nature Futures Framework, Three Horizons Framework, and X-curve to translate diverse values and knowledge systems into transformation pathways.
  • Contribution to transformative change: Moves beyond documenting ILK by demonstrating its potential to shape collective action and contribute to long-term social-ecological transformations towards sustainable mangrove futures.

Title: MSP4BIODIVERSITY project: co-construction and analysis of scenarios to mainstream biodiversity conservation into Maritime Spatial Planning
Subnational Region: The Northern Adriatic Sea (NAS), the Strait of Sicily (SoS), and the Northern Tyrrhenian and Ligurian Sea (NTS).
Intro: MSP4BIODIVERSITY: mainstreaming biodiversity protection into MSP in Italy through co-constructed scenario
Description:
The MSP4BIODIVERSITY project (2023-2026) was funded through Italy's National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR) and coordinated by the National Research Council of Italy under Spoke 2 of the National Biodiversity Future Centre. It aimed at integrating biodiversity into Italian Maritime Spatial Planning (MSP). Rather than treating environmental protection as an external constraint, the project positions ecosystem health, biodiversity, and ecosystem services as core components of marine governance to reconcile maritime uses with long-term ecosystem resilience and the EU Biodiversity Strategy 2030. The project used scenario co-construction and participatory analysis, grounded in the Social-Ecological System (SES) framework, to explore marine management options, trade-offs, and uncertainties. Scenarios were developed in a real-world context, across three Italian pilot areas: The Northern Adriatic Sea (NAS), the Strait of Sicily (SoS), and the Northern Tyrrhenian and Ligurian Sea (NTS).

For each pilot area, three distinct, spatially explicit scenarios were co-constructed using a mixed qualitative and quantitative approach that blends policy analysis, scientific modelling, expert judgment, and stakeholder engagement. The "Slow Pace" scenario projects the continuation of existing environmental management trajectories; the "Nature@Work" scenario prioritises biodiversity conservation, ecosystem restoration, and expanded area-based protection; and the "Blue Development" scenario explores innovation, sustainable blue economy growth, and "building with nature" approaches. Each scenario is composed of narratives depicting the evolution at 2040 of sea uses: maritime transport and ports; energy; coastal defence; fisheries; aquaculture; coastal and maritime tourism; research and innovation; maritime safety and surveillance; and nature protection. Scenarios are also composed of maps representing the distribution of these uses and related management measures.

A strong co-development approach, involving local stakeholders in each of the pilot areas, was adopted for the scenarios’ formulation. Once developed, scenarios were used as input to a diversified suite of models to evaluate their social, economic and environmental effects. Results were then discussed with stakeholders in workshops focusing on participatory, multi-dimensional analysis of scenarios, based on a 10-tenet model.
Impact: A national workshop was organised in Rome on 31 March 2026 to discuss the transferability of the results of the MSP4BIODIVERSITY project to the Italian Maritime Spatial Plan process. The discussion focused on whether, and under which conditions, the co-construction approach developed by the project and its main outputs (scenario narratives and their spatial measures, modelling results of the analysis of the effects of these scenarios, and the integrated and participatory evaluation of the scenarios based on the integration of stakeholder evaluation and the analysis of the modelling results) effectively support the implementation, monitoring and future adaptive updating of MSP in Italy. The workshop was conceived as an implementation-oriented moment, moving beyond the technical development of scenarios and analyses to consider their practical usability for competent authorities, planners, and experts.

Title: Urban transformation pathways towards a safe and just future in Monterrey, Mexico
Intro: This case details a participatory visioning workshop that explored sustainable futures for Monterrey, Mexico, bounded under the Safe and Just Earth system boundaries framework.
Description:
This project aimed to engage a diverse group of local stakeholders from the Monterrey Metropolitan area to co-create visions and pathways towards safe and just futures for the city. We collaboratively created a local safe and just Earth system boundaries model for the city, and then explored visions and transformation pathways to achieve a future within these locally identified boundaries.

Three distinct visions emerged, reconceptualizing the city’s relationship between nature and society, and each with unique pathway dynamics. These pathways call for cultural, economic and social paradigm shifts, underscored the fragility of transformation, trade-offs across boundaries and scales, and the need to address systemic inequalities to achieve transformative change.

Insights from the study were shared with these local stakeholders to inform decision-making. The research also contributed as a local case study of transformation pathways for the Earth Commission's ongoing work on safe and just boundaries, offering concrete avenues for change for Monterrey while challenging the assumptions that guide global scenario-making processes.
Impact: The study catalyzed further futures-focused initiatives by workshop participants, and is being used as a local case study within Earth Commission Transformation Pathways working group
